'''Amani Askari Toomer''' (born September 8, 1974) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who spent his entire career as a [[wide receiver]] and [[punt returner]] for the [[New York Giants]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He registered over 1,000 receiving yards each season from 1999 to 2003, was a member of the [[2007 New York Giants season|2007 Giants team]] that won [[Super Bowl XLII]], and holds Giants' club records with 9,497 receiving yards, 668 [[Reception (gridiron football)|receptions]], and 54 receiving [[touchdown]]s. He also returned 109 punts for 1,060 yards and three touchdowns.  As a rookie in 1996, he led the NFL with an average of 16.6 yards on 18 punt returns.	

Toomer played [[college football]] for the [[Michigan Wolverines football|Michigan Wolverines]] from 1992 to 1995. In 1994, he broke the school's single-season record with 1,096 receiving yards and was a finalist for the [[Biletnikoff Award]] and a first-team [[1994 All-Big Ten Conference football team|All-Big Ten]] honoree. Toomer finished his college career ranked second (now fourth) in Michigan history with 2,657 receiving yards.

==Early life==
Toomer was born in [[Berkeley, California]], in 1974.<ref name=PFR>{{cite web|title=Amani Toomer NFL Statistics|publisher=Sports Reference LLC|work=Pro-Football-Reference.com|access-date=April 13, 2015|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/T/ToomAm00.htm}}</ref>  His first name, "Amani", is Swahili for peace, and his middle name, "Askari", is Swahili for soldier.<ref name=PAS>{{cite web|title=Amani Toomer Profile and Stats|publisher=Amani Toomer|work=amanitoomer81.com|access-date=April 13, 2015|url=http://amanitoomer81.com/profile}}</ref>  Toomer's father, Donald Toomer, played [[college football]] for [[Woody Hayes]] at [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Ohio State]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Learning and Teaching Never Seem to End for the Giants' Toomer|newspaper=The New York Times|date=November 1, 2008|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/11/02/sports/football/02giants.html}}</ref> His uncle is comedian [[George Wallace (American comedian)|George Wallace]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Super Bowl ring to have company|date=January 23, 2008|newspaper=Las Vegas Review-Journal|url=http://www.reviewjournal.com/norm-clarke/super-bowl-ring-have-company}}</ref> Toomer began playing [[Pee-Wee Football]] as a [[Lineman (American football)|lineman]] for the Berkeley Cougars and as a receiver, [[Placekicker|kicker]], [[Punter (football)|punter]], [[linebacker]], and [[running back]] for the Richmond Steelers.<ref name=PAS/>

Toomer attended [[De La Salle High School (Concord, California)|De La Salle High School]] in [[Concord, California]]. As a football player at De La Salle, Toomer was selected as a ''[[Parade (magazine)|Parade]]'' All-American and a ''[[USA Today]]'' [[1991 USA Today All-USA high school football team|All-USA]] player.<ref name=ESPN15>{{cite news|title=Amani Toomer among top Spartans|work=ESPN.com|date=September 22, 2011|url=https://www.espn.com/college-sports/recruiting/football/story/_/id/7001261/top-15-players-de-la-salle}}</ref>

==University of Michigan==
Toomer enrolled at the [[University of Michigan]] in 1992 and played [[college football]] for the [[Michigan Wolverines football]] team from 1992 to 1995.<ref name=Roster>{{cite web|title=Michigan Football Roster Database|publisher=University of Michigan, Bentley Historical Library|access-date=April 12, 2015|url=https://bentley.umich.edu/athdept/rosters/football.php}}</ref>  As a freshman and sophomore in 1992 and 1993, he started only three games (two in 1992 and one in 1993) and was principally used as a backup to the team's #1 receiver, [[Derrick Alexander (wide receiver)|Derrick Alexander]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://bentley.umich.edu/athdept/football/fbteam/1992fbt.htm|title=1992 Football Team|publisher=University of Michigan, Bentley Historical Library |access-date=April 13, 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://bentley.umich.edu/athdept/football/fbteam/1993fbt.htm|title=1993 Football Team|publisher=University of Michigan, Bentley Historical Library |access-date=April 13, 2015}}</ref> Toomer caught 16 passes for 238 yards in 1992 and 29 passes for 565 yards in 1993.<ref name=Stat>{{cite web|title=Michigan Football Statistic Archive Query Page |publisher=University of Michigan |access-date=April 13, 2015 |url=http://stats.ath.umich.edu/football/footstart.php |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040907204739/http://stats.ath.umich.edu/football/footstart.php |archive-date=September 7, 2004 }}(to retrieve Toomer's college statistics, enter "toomer" in the box for the player's last name)</ref>

===1994 season===
As a junior in 1994, Toomer did not start any games for Michigan, as [[Mercury Hayes]] was the starting flanker in all 12 games.<ref name=t94>{{cite web|url=https://bentley.umich.edu/athdept/football/fbteam/1994fbt.htm|title=1994 Football Team|publisher=University of Michigan, Bentley Historical Library |access-date=April 13, 2015}}</ref>  Despite technically being a "backup" to Hayes, Toomer in 1994 broke [[Jack Clancy]]'s single-season Michigan record with 1,096 receiving yards.<ref>{{cite web|title=Michigan Football Statistic Archive Query Page |publisher=University of Michigan |access-date=April 13, 2015 |url=http://stats.ath.umich.edu/football/footstart.php |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040907204739/http://stats.ath.umich.edu/football/footstart.php |archive-date=September 7, 2004 }}(To retrieve a list of Michigan's leading single-season receiving leaders, go to the section for "Individual Statistical Leaders" and select the dropdowns for Season Receiving Yards. As of the end of the 2014 season, six players led by [[Jeremy Gallon]] have now surpassed Toomer's 1994 receiving yardage.)</ref><ref name=Boom>{{cite news|title=Boomerang: Amani Toomer keeps coming back to Michigan|newspaper=The Michigan Daily|date=September 7, 1995|page=15|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2706&dat=19950907&id=-A9KAAAAIBAJ&sjid=sB4NAAAAIBAJ&pg=3618,614582&hl=en}}</ref> With [[Todd Collins (quarterback)|Todd Collins]] at quarterback, Toomer was the [[1994 Michigan Wolverines football team|1994 Wolverines]]' leading receiver with 54 receptions for 1,096 yards, an average of 20.3 yards per reception.<ref name=Stat/>  Toomer also finished the season as the [[Big Ten Conference]]'s leading receiver with an average of 93.9 receiving yards per game.<ref name=Boom/>  He had a career-high 179 receiving yards, including touchdown receptions of 46 and 38 yards, in the Wolverines' 1994 season-opening victory over [[Boston College]].<ref name=Stat/><ref>{{cite news|title=Michigan rallies past Boston College|newspaper=Spartanburg Herald-Journal (AP story)|date=September 4, 1994|page=D4|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1876&dat=19940904&id=vOseAAAAIBAJ&sjid=R88EAAAAIBAJ&pg=6666,769997&hl=en}}</ref> He also returned a punt 72 yards for a touchdown against [[Illinois Fighting Illini football|Illinois]].<ref>{{cite news|title=No. 11 Michigan 19, Illinois 14|newspaper=Star-News|date=October 23, 1994|page=4C|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1454&dat=19941023&id=gvZOAAAAIBAJ&sjid=BhUEAAAAIBAJ&pg=6065,3096305&hl=en}}</ref> Toomer was a finalist for the [[Biletnikoff Award]] in 1994 and was selected by both the conference coaches and media as a first-team wide receiver on the [[1994 All-Big Ten Conference football team|1994 All-Big Ten team]].<ref name=Boom/>

===1995 season===
As a senior, Toomer finally became a starter, starting 12 games at split end for the [[1995 Michigan Wolverines football team|1995 Michigan team]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://bentley.umich.edu/athdept/football/fbteam/1995bt.htm|title=1995 Football Team|publisher=University of Michigan, Bentley Historical Library|access-date=April 13, 2015}}{{Dead link|date=October 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>  However, Toomer was routinely double-teamed in 1995,<ref>{{cite news|title=Giant rookie and rookie Giant: Wolverine alum wide receiver Toomer displays size, skill|newspaper=The Michigan Daily|date=August 14, 1996|page=15|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2706&dat=19960814&id=KwBKAAAAIBAJ&sjid=NB4NAAAAIBAJ&pg=1843,5710941&hl=en}}</ref> opening the way for [[Mercury Hayes]] to lead the team in both receptions and receiving yardage.  Toomer finished the 1995 season with 44 receptions for 758 yards and seven touchdowns.<ref name=Stat/>  He had his best game of the season in a 52–17 victory over [[1995 Minnesota Golden Gophers football team|Minnesota]], catching five passes for 174 yards and two touchdowns, including a career-long 75-yard touchdown reception from [[Brian Griese]].<ref name=Stat/><ref>{{cite news|title=Michigan blasts Minnesota, 52-17: Toomer, Biakabutuka shine|newspaper=The Michigan Daily|date=October 30, 1995|page=1B|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2706&dat=19951030&id=FBBKAAAAIBAJ&sjid=sB4NAAAAIBAJ&pg=2166,3316606&hl=en}}</ref>

===College career overview===
In four seasons at Michigan, Toomer had 124 receptions for 2,144 yards (17.3 per catch) and 12 receiving touchdowns.<ref name=Stat/> He finished his college career ranked second (now fourth) in Michigan history with 2,657 receiving yards.<ref>{{cite web|title=Michigan Football Statistic Archive Query Page |publisher=University of Michigan |access-date=April 13, 2015 |url=http://stats.ath.umich.edu/football/footstart.php |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040907204739/http://stats.ath.umich.edu/football/footstart.php |archive-date=September 7, 2004 }}(To retrieve a list of Michigan's leading career receiving leaders, go to the section for "Individual Statistical Leaders" and select the dropdowns for Career Receiving Yards.)</ref> Toomer was also used as a [[punt returner|punt]] and [[kick returner]] at Michigan.  He returned 46 punts for 384 yards (8.3 yards per return) and two touchdowns.  He also returned 14 kickoffs for 306 yards (21.9 yards per return).<ref name=Stat/>

===Return specialist: 1996–1998===
Toomer was selected by the [[New York Giants]] in the second round (34th overall pick) of the [[1996 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1996 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1996/draft.htm |access-date=March 30, 2023 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>  In July 1996, he signed a three-year contract with the Giants providing a $670,000 signing bonus and salaries of $269,000 in 1996, $336,000 in 1997, and $403,000 in 1998.<ref>{{cite news|title=Giants Sign Second Pick|newspaper=The New York Times|date=July 22, 1996|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1996/07/22/sports/pro-football-giants-sign-second-pick.html}}</ref>

In his first three seasons with the Giants, Toomer was principally used as a [[punt returner|punt]] and [[kickoff returner]]. In his first NFL game, the opening game of the [[1996 New York Giants season|1996 season]], Toomer set a Giants' record with an 87-yard punt return for a touchdown against the [[Buffalo Bills]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Toomer Shakes Jitters And Catches On Fast|newspaper=The New York Times|date=September 7, 1996}}</ref>  He returned a second punt for a touchdown that season against the [[Philadelphia Eagles]], before injuring his [[anterior cruciate ligament]] (ACL) and spending the rest of the season on [[injured reserve]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Giants Are Still Feeling Toomer's Injury Exit|newspaper=The New York Times|date=December 6, 1996}}</ref>  Toomer led the NFL in 1996 with an average of 16.1 yards on 19 punt returns.<ref name=PFR/>

During the [[1997 New York Giants season|1997 season]], Toomer appeared in all 16 games for the Giants and returned 47 punts for 455 yards, an average of 9.7 yards per return.<ref name=PFR/>  He registered his third punt return touchdown. He also caught his first touchdown pass on November 16, 1997, a 56-yard reception from [[Danny Kanell]] against the [[Arizona Cardinals]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Few Points for Artistry, but Giants Show They Can Bounce Back|newspaper=New York Times|date=November 17, 1997|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1997/11/17/sports/pro-football-few-points-for-artistry-but-giants-show-they-can-bounce-back.html}}</ref>

In [[1998 New York Giants season|1998]], Toomer again appeared in all 16 games for the Giants.  He returned 35 punts for 252 yards, an average of 7.1 yards per return.  He also began to see increased playing time as a receiver, registering 27 catches for 360 yards and five touchdowns.<ref name=PFR/>  In Week 15, in a come-from-behind victory over the previously undefeated [[Denver Broncos]], Toomer caught a 37-yard touchdown pass from [[Kent Graham]] with 48 seconds left in the game as the Giants ruined the Broncos' dream of a perfect season by winning 20–16.<ref>{{cite news|title=Broncos Perfect No Longer; Giants Win|newspaper=Lakeland Ledger (AP story)|date=December 14, 1998|page=C1|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1346&dat=19981214&id=Qr0wAAAAIBAJ&sjid=z_wDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6281,4993707&hl=en}}</ref> Toomer later publicly acknowledged that his slow start as an NFL receiver was the result of exercise-induced [[asthma]] which he had hidden for years.  After seeking treatment for the condition, his receiving career blossomed in 1999 and 2000.<ref>{{cite news|title=NFL's Amani Toomer wins big against asthma|date=October 22, 2001|newspaper=USA Today|url=http://usatoday30.usatoday.com/news/health/spotlight/2001-10-22-toomer-asthma.htm}}</ref>

===Prime years: 1999–2003===
During the [[1999 New York Giants season]], Toomer became a starting wide receiver in all 16 games. That year, he broke the team record for receptions in a season (79), and his 1,183 receiving yards were the second-highest in team history behind [[Homer Jones (American football)|Homer Jones]].

In 2000, Toomer appeared in all 16 regular season games (14 as a starter) for the Giants and posted solid totals with 78 receptions for 1,094 yards and seven touchdowns.<ref name=PFR/> With [[Kerry Collins]] at [[quarterback]], the [[2000 New York Giants season|2000 Giants team]] advanced to [[Super Bowl XXXV]] (a loss to the [[Baltimore Ravens]]), and Toomer started all three postseason games for the team.  He totaled 10 catches for 135 yards and a touchdown in the [[2000–01 NFL playoffs]].<ref name=PFR/>

During the [[2001 New York Giants season]], Toomer appeared in all 16 regular season games, caught more than 70 passes, and gained over 1,000 receiving yards for the third consecutive year.<ref name=PFR/>

Toomer had the best year of his NFL career in [[2002 New York Giants season|2002]].  He set Giants' single-season records with 82 receptions and 1,343 receiving yards.  His eight receiving touchdowns in 2002 were also a career-high. His total of 204 receiving yards against the [[Indianapolis Colts]] was also the highest total for a Giants wide receiver in a 60-minute game (two players had higher receiving totals, but both of those games went to [[Overtime (sports)|overtime]]).

In [[2003 New York Giants season|2003]], Toomer started all 16 games and had his fifth consecutive season with at least 1,000 receiving yards.  He totaled 63 catches for 1,057 yards and five touchdowns.<ref name=PFR/>  In the second game of the season, a Monday night game against the [[Dallas Cowboys]], Toomer broke [[Frank Gifford]]'s club record for receiving yardage.<ref>{{cite news|title=Homecoming sweet for Parcells|newspaper=McCook Daily Gazette|date=September 16, 2003|page=12|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1933&dat=20030910&id=2qggAAAAIBAJ&sjid=ZmkFAAAAIBAJ&pg=1480,2153490&hl=en}}</ref>

===2004–2006===
The [[2004 New York Giants season|2004 season]] marked the first time since Toomer's rookie year in which he did not score a touchdown.  Toomer appeared in 15 games and had 51 catches for 747 yards, the sixth consecutive season in which he topped 50 catches and 700 yards.<ref name=PFR/>

During the [[2005 New York Giants season|2005 season]], the Giants had a new starting quarterback, [[Eli Manning]], who threw for almost 3,800 yards. [[Plaxico Burress]] took over as the Giants' #1 receiver, but Toomer still started all 16 games and had 60 receptions for 684 yards and seven touchdowns.<ref name=PFR/>  Toomer's 2005 highlights included a last-second touchdown reception against the Denver Broncos, a late game-tying touchdown at Seattle, and a fourth-and-goal touchdown catch against the Rams.

Toomer started strongly in the [[2006 New York Giants season|2006 season]].  In a Week 2 game against the [[Philadelphia Eagles]], he tallied a career-high 12 receptions and scored two touchdowns to help spark a 17-point comeback.  Physically exhausted by game's end, he had to be carried off the field by trainers.<ref name=Quiet/> Toomer's season came to an end after eight games when he suffered a partially torn [[Anterior cruciate ligament injury|ACL]] in his left knee.<ref>{{cite news|title=Setbacks for Giants Spread as Toomer Is Out for Season|date=November 9, 2006|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/11/09/sports/football/09giants.html}}</ref> In eight games during the 2006 season, Toomer had 32 receptions for 360 yards and three touchdowns.<ref name=PFR/>  The Giants compiled a 6–2 record in the first half of the season with Toomer in the lineup, but fell to 2–6 in the second half without Toomer.  Giants head coach [[Tom Coughlin]] noted, "There's no question Amani has a very positive effect on Eli."<ref name=NYT07/>  Quarterback [[Eli Manning]] also praised Toomer: "He has a way of being in the right place at the right time."<ref name=NYT07>{{cite news|title=Toomer Thrives in Right Place at Right Time|date=August 19, 2007|newspaper=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/08/19/sports/football/19giants.html}}</ref>

===Super Bowl champion: 2007===
[[File:George W. Bush meets with NY Giants 20080430-6 p043008sc-0510-515h.jpg|thumb|right|200px|Amani presenting George W. Bush with a personalized Giants jersey on April 30, 2008.<ref name="whitehouse"/>]]

During the [[2007 NFL season|2007 season]], Toomer returned from his injury to appear in all 16 regular season games for the Giants.  He totaled 59 receptions for 760 yards and three touchdowns. On October 21, 2007, in a home game against the [[San Francisco 49ers]], he broke [[Kyle Rote]]'s club record with his 49th career touchdown catch.<ref>{{cite news|title=Setting Records Is Not the Priority for Toomer|date=October 22, 2007|newspaper=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/10/22/sports/football/22araton.html}}</ref> In the same game, he also broke [[Tiki Barber]]'s team record for career receptions.<ref>{{cite news|title=Giants' Toomer Excels With a Body of Work|newspaper=The New York Times|date=October 18, 2007|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/10/18/sports/football/18giants.html}}</ref>

The [[2007 New York Giants season|2007 Giants]] advanced through the playoffs and won [[Super Bowl XLII]] over the previously undefeated [[2007 New England Patriots season|New England Patriots]]. Toomer started all four postseason games for the team and totaled 21 catches for 280 yards and three touchdowns.<ref name=PFR/> On January 13, 2008, during the [[2007–08 NFL playoffs|2007 divisional playoff round]], Toomer caught a 52-yard touchdown pass, his longest since a 77-yard touchdown on November 30, 2003.  This catch broke the club record for most postseason receptions. Toomer had two touchdown catches in the Giants' 21–17 upset over the [[2007 Dallas Cowboys season|Dallas Cowboys]]. His first touchdown gave the Giants a 7–0 lead after he caught an 11-yard pass, eluded three would be tacklers, and ran 50 yards for the score. Toomer also led the Giants with six receptions for 84 yards in the Super Bowl. In May 2008, Toomer and the Giants were invited by [[U.S President]] [[George W. Bush]] to the [[White House]] to honor their victory in Super Bowl XLII.<ref name="whitehouse">{{cite web|url=https://georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov/news/releases/2008/04/20080430-6.html|title=President Bush Welcomes Super Bowl XLII Champion New York Giants to White House|author=Office of the Press Secretary|publisher=The White House|access-date=April 30, 2008|date=April 30, 2008}}</ref>

===2008 season and career overview===
The [[2008 New York Giants season|2008 season]] was Toomer's last in the NFL. He appeared in all 16 regular season games, 12 as a starter, and caught 48 passes for 580 yards and four touchdowns.  He concluded his NFL career having appeared in 190 games, 142 as a starter, with 668 receptions for 9,497 yards (14.2 yards per catch), and 54 touchdown receptions.<ref name=PFR/>  He holds Giants' record for most career receiving yards, receptions, receiving touchdowns, and most consecutive games with at least one reception (94).<ref>{{cite web|title=New York Giants Receiving Career Leaders|publisher=Sports Reference LLC|work=Pro-Football-Reference.com|access-date=April 13, 2015|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/nyg/career-receiving.htm}}</ref><ref name=Quiet>{{cite news|title=The Quiet Giant Who Catches Passes, Not Praise|date=September 21, 2006|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/09/21/sports/football/21giants.html}}</ref> In 2010, Toomer was included in the initial group selected for induction into the [[New York Giants#Ring of Honor|New York Giants Ring of Honor]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Tiki Barber showered with boos at Giants Ring of Honor ceremony|newspaper=New York Daily News|date=October 4, 2010|url=http://www.nydailynews.com/sports/football/giants/tiki-barber-showered-boos-giants-ring-honor-ceremony-punter-matt-dodge-struggling-article-1.186098}}</ref>

====Giants franchise records====
{{As of|2017}}'s NFL off-season, Amani Toomer held at least 16 Giants franchise records, including:
* Most Receptions (career): 668
* Most Receptions (game): 12 (2006-09-17 @PHI; tied with [[Mark Bavaro]], [[Hakeem Nicks]] and [[Odell Beckham Jr.]] x2)
* Most Receptions (playoff career): 44
* Most Receiving Yds (career): 9,497
* Most Receiving Yds (playoff career): 608
* Most Receiving TDs (career): 54
* Most Receiving TDs (playoff career): 7
* Most Receiving TDs (playoff game): 3 (2003-01-05 @SFO)
* Most Total TDs (playoff career): 7
* Most Total TDs (playoff game): 3 (2003-01-05 @SFO)
* Most Punt Returns (season): 47 (1997; tied with [[Chad Morton]])
* Most 100+ yard receiving games (career): 23
* Most Games with 1+ TD scored (playoffs): 4 (tied with [[Brandon Jacobs]])
* Most Games with 2+ TD scored (playoffs): 2 (tied with [[Hakeem Nicks]])
* Most Games with 3+ TD scored (playoffs): 1
* Most 1000+ receiving yards (career): 5

===Kansas City Chiefs===
Toomer was signed to a one-year contract by [[Kansas City Chiefs]] on August 4, 2009.<ref name="chiefs">{{cite web|url=http://www.nfl.com/trainingcamp/story?id=09000d5d811a881c&template=with-video-with-comments&confirm=true|title=Veteran WR Toomer practices with Chiefs after signing one-year deal|author=NFL.com Wire Reports|work=NFL.com|access-date=August 5, 2009|date=August 5, 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090806161339/http://www.nfl.com/trainingcamp/story?id=09000d5d811a881c&template=with-video-with-comments&confirm=true|archive-date=August 6, 2009|url-status=dead}}</ref> He was released during final roster cuts on September 1.<ref>{{cite web|title=Chiefs release Amani Toomer|url=http://www.nypost.com/p/blogs/backpage/item_XWwYnnUkrKpkKMFl2N74QN|publisher=New York Post|access-date=May 18, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121023035026/http://www.nypost.com/p/blogs/backpage/item_XWwYnnUkrKpkKMFl2N74QN|archive-date=October 23, 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Personal life and post-playing career==
In 2011, Toomer and fellow former New York Giant [[Roman Oben]] joined [[MSG Network|MSG]] Varsity's coverage of "Friday Night Football."<ref name="MSG Varsity">{{cite web|url=http://www.msgvarsity.com/press/msg-varsity-takes-a-giant-step-forward-1.566606|title=MSG Varsity takes a 'Giant' step forward|author=MSGVarsity.com|publisher=MSG Varsity|date=August 25, 2011|access-date=August 29, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927084746/http://www.msgvarsity.com/press/msg-varsity-takes-a-giant-step-forward-1.566606|archive-date=September 27, 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 2012, he joined [[NBC Sports Radio]] where he was a  co-host with Dan Schwartzman of "[[Going Deep with Amani and Dan]]", a nighttime talk show on the network.<ref>{{cite web|title=Amani Toomer profile|publisher=NBC Sports Group|access-date=April 14, 2015|url=http://nbcsportsgrouppressbox.com/bio/amani-toomer/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150327135620/http://nbcsportsgrouppressbox.com/bio/amani-toomer/|archive-date=March 27, 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref> Toomer lived in [[Weehawken, New Jersey]].<ref>{{cite web | last=Strunsky | first=Steve | title=Giants great Amani Toomer and Weehawken group notch revaluation victory | website=NJ.com| date=2015-11-17 | url=https://www.nj.com/hudson/2015/11/giants_great_amani_toomer_scores_in_weehawken_reva.html | access-date=2025-07-04}}</ref>

In the summer of 2020, Toomer, along with his Danish wife Maj and their 3 children relocated to [[Ebeltoft]], [[Denmark]], because of the [[COVID-19 pandemic]]. During the [[2020 NFL season]] he worked as an expert on [[TV3 Sport]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bt.dk/sport/amerikansk-sportsstjerne-er-flyttet-til-ebeltoft|title=Amerikansk sportsstjerne er flyttet til Ebeltoft|date=September 25, 2020}}</ref>

'''Francis Alvin Pearman, II''' (born August 10, 1982) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).  He played [[college football]] for the [[Virginia Cavaliers football|Virginia Cavaliers]] and was selected by the [[Jacksonville Jaguars]] in the fourth round of the [[2005 NFL draft]]. During his NFL career, he played for the Jaguars, [[Seattle Seahawks]], and [[Tennessee Titans]]. He received his B.S. from the [[University of Virginia]] in 2005.{{Cn|date=April 2025}}

==Professional career==

===Jacksonville Jaguars (first stint)===
Pearman was selected by the [[Jacksonville Jaguars]] in the fourth round (127th overall) of the [[2005 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2005 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2005/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-07 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He wore number 34 while with the team.

As a rookie, Pearman carried the ball 39 times for 149 yards and a touchdown. He also caught 32 passes for 240 yards.  Pearman handled the bulk of the team's punt returns during the season, averaging 8.4 yards on 49 attempts. He finished the 2005 regular season with 986 all-purpose yards.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Alvin Pearman 2005 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/P/PearAl00/gamelog/2005/ |access-date=2025-06-29 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> In his first NFL game, he forced a fumble on the opening kickoff which ultimately led to a field goal.

===Seattle Seahawks===
On September 1, 2007, Pearman was traded to the [[Seattle Seahawks]] for a sixth-round draft choice. After suffering a knee injury, the team placed him on injured reserve on October 2, 2007.

===Jacksonville Jaguars (second stint)===
Pearman was re-signed by the Jaguars on December 11, 2008, after [[running back]] [[Fred Taylor (running back)|Fred Taylor]] was placed on [[injured reserve]]. Pearman scored a 23-yard receiving touchdown, his only reception of the season, in the season finale against the [[Baltimore Ravens]]. The team waived Pearman on September 5, 2009.

===Tennessee Titans===
Pearman signed with the [[Tennessee Titans]] on October 30, 2009, and was assigned jersey number 35. During the 2009 season, Pearman played in 5 games, returned 11 punts for 112 yards (10.2 average) and 8 kickoffs for 174 yards (21.8 average). He also registered 4 tackles.  At the start of the 2010–2011 season, Pearman was listed as third on the team's running back depth chart behind Chris Johnson and Javon Ringer.

==Personal life==
At the conclusion of his NFL career, Pearman earned a M.Ed. and Ph.D. from [[Vanderbilt University]]. He is currently an assistant professor of education in the Graduate School of Education at [[Stanford University]]. He was previously a professor of Urban Education at the [[University of Pittsburgh]].

'''Amos L. Zereoué''' (born October 8, 1976) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[West Virginia Mountaineers football|West Virginia Mountaineers]]. He was selected by the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] in the third round of the [[1999 NFL draft]]. He also played for the [[Oakland Raiders]] and [[New England Patriots]].

He owned and operated a restaurant in [[Manhattan, New York]], called Zereoué.<ref name="Restaurant">{{cite web |url=http://www.timeswv.com/wvu_sports/local_story_171022418.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20090627093047/http://www.timeswv.com/wvu_sports/local_story_171022418.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=June 27, 2009 |title=WVU's Famous Amos cooks up a new career |first=Bob |last=Hertzel |work=TimesWV.com |publisher=[[Times West Virginian]] |date=June 20, 2009 |accessdate=June 20, 2009}}</ref> It has since closed.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.lostlettermen.com/article/amos-zereoue-tries-his-hand-at-soccer-restaurant-business |title=Ex-WVU's Amos Zereoue Active in Retirement - Lost Lettermen |accessdate=October 1, 2014 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20141006124157/http://www.lostlettermen.com/article/amos-zereoue-tries-his-hand-at-soccer-restaurant-business |archivedate=October 6, 2014}}</ref>

==Early life==
Zereoué was raised by a single father in [[Hempstead (village), New York|Hempstead, New York]]; he lived in a group home called "Hope for Youth", in Bellmore, NY, during his high school years, owing to legal trouble in junior high school and the concerns of his father that the drugs and crime of the neighborhood he grew up in were undermining his ambition.<ref name=zer>{{cite web|url=http://www.ia.wvu.edu/~magazine/spring99/htmlfiles/amos.html |title=Amos Zereoue's Achievements |publisher=Ia.wvu.edu |accessdate=September 22, 2010 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100628072032/http://www.ia.wvu.edu/~magazine/spring99/htmlfiles/amos.html |archivedate=June 28, 2010 }}</ref>

Zereoué attended [[Wellington C. Mepham High School]] in [[Bellmore, New York]], and was a [[Varsity letter|letterman]] in [[High school football|football]]. He set [[Long Island]] records of 5,360 yards and 59 [[touchdown]]s at Mepham, earning [[Street & Smith]] All-America recognition. He was also the first two-time Thorpe Award winner in high school, which recognizes the best player in [[Nassau County, New York|Nassau County]], an honor that surpassed local icons such as [[Jim Brown]] and [[Matt Snell]].<ref name=zer /><ref name="Patriots bio">{{cite web|url=http://www.patriots.com/team/index.cfm?ac=playerbio&bio=31442 |title=Amos Zereoue - Official New England Patriots Biography |publisher=Patriots.com |accessdate=September 22, 2010 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090314000321/http://www.patriots.com/team/index.cfm?ac=playerbio&bio=31442 |archivedate=March 14, 2009 }}</ref>

==College career==
===Freshman (1996)===
Zereoué was a late addition to the [[West Virginia Mountaineers football|West Virginia]] roster in [[1996 West Virginia Mountaineers football team|1996]], but made an immediate impact. On his first collegiate carry, he rushed the ball for a 69-yard touchdown against [[Pitt Panthers football|Pitt]].<ref name="Restaurant" /> In that same season, he finished the season with two of the school's five-best single-game rushing performances (234 yards against [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish football|Notre Dame]] and 228 yards against [[Rutgers Scarlet Knights football|Rutgers]]). He was unanimously voted the [[Big East Conference (1979–2013)|Big East]] Rookie of the Year after the season and was a First-team All-Big East selection. He also set a West Virginia freshman rushing record for a season with 1,035 rushing yards, which was later broken by his successor, [[Avon Cobourne]] (who broke Zereoué's career rushing records as well).<ref name="Patriots bio" />

===Sophomore (1997)===
Zereoué was tenth in the [[1997 NCAA Division I-A football season#Heisman Trophy|1997]] [[Heisman Trophy]] race and was a [[Doak Walker Award]] semifinalist. He was a third-team [[All-American]] selection and was voted all-Big East and first-team All-[[Eastern College Athletic Conference|ECAC]] selection as well. He also led the conference and set a school single-season rushing record with 1,589 yards on 281 carries. His 18 touchdowns on the [[1997 West Virginia Mountaineers football team|season]] was one shy of the school record. He was ranked third on the season with 150 yards-per-game.<ref name="Patriots bio" />

===Junior (1998)===
Zereoué was a Second-team All-American selection in [[1998 West Virginia Mountaineers football team|1998]] by leading the team with 1,462 yards and 13 touchdowns on 283 carries. He was also ranked sixth in the nation with 143 yards-per-game in 1998.<ref name="Patriots bio" />

During his college career, he rushed for over 100 yards 21 times, had seven straight games with over 100 yards rushing - averaging 123.8 yards-per-game during his career. At the time of leaving, he held the all-time school rushing yardage with 4,086 and held the record for the most yards in a season with 1,589 in 1997. Both records were broken by his successor at running back, Avon Cobourne. While at West Virginia Zereoué's nickname was "Famous Amos".

==Professional career==
===Pittsburgh Steelers (1999–2003)===
Zereoué was selected in the third round, 95th overall of the [[1999 NFL draft]] by the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]], who had acquired future-[[Pro Football Hall of Fame|Hall of Famer]] [[Jerome Bettis]] from the [[St. Louis Rams]] four years earlier in 1996.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1999 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1999/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-28 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Zereoué got good playing time in his five seasons in Pittsburgh from 1999 to 2003. His best season came in [[2002 Pittsburgh Steelers season|2002]], when he rushed for a career-high 762 yards and four touchdowns. Also in 2002, he caught a career-high 42 receptions for 341 yards. In his years in Pittsburgh, he rushed for 1,698 yards and seven touchdowns.<ref name="Patriots bio" />

===Oakland Raiders (2004)===
After the [[2003 Pittsburgh Steelers season|2003 season]], Zereoué was cut by the Steelers. He was then signed as a [[free-agent]] by the [[Oakland Raiders]]. [[Tyrone Wheatley]] ended up getting the starting job for [[2004 Oakland Raiders season|2004]], but Zereoué saw time on the field as well. He rushed for 425 yards and three touchdowns in his one season in Oakland, before he was cut with the arrival of [[LaMont Jordan]] from the [[New York Jets]].<ref name="Patriots bio" />

===New England Patriots (2005)===
After being cut by the Raiders, Zereoué spent his final [[2005 New England Patriots season|NFL season]] with the [[New England Patriots]]. He spent time playing backup to veteran [[Corey Dillon]], but he only ran the ball seven times on the season for 14 yards. He then was cut by the Patriots as well, and eventually retired.<ref name="Patriots bio" />
[[File:Zereoues.jpg|right|thumb|Zereoué restaurant interior, 2008.]]
In his seven-year career, Zereoué rushed for 2,137 yards with 10 touchdowns. He caught 137 receptions for 1,111 yards and a touchdown. He also had seven kick returns for 169 yards.

'''Amon Gordon''' (born October 13, 1981) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[Cleveland Browns]] in the fourth round of the [[2004 NFL draft]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Stanford Cardinal football|Stanford Cardinal]].

Gordon was also a member of the [[Denver Broncos]], [[Baltimore Ravens]], [[Tennessee Titans]], [[Philadelphia Eagles]], [[New England Patriots]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://archive.patriots.com/team/index.cfm?ac=playerbio&bio=34178|title=The New England Patriots: Amon Gordon|accessdate=21 January 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160118234659/http://archive.patriots.com/team/index.cfm?ac=playerbio&bio=34178|archive-date=18 January 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> [[Seattle Seahawks]], [[Houston Texans]] and [[Kansas City Chiefs]].

==Early life==
Gordon attended [[Oak Harbor High School (Washington)|Oak Harbor High School]] in Washington state, where he was the only Freshman on the varsity football and basketball teams.  After his freshman year, Gordon transferred to [[Mariner High School (Everett, Washington)|Mariner High School]], in [[Everett, Washington]] and played football there as a sophomore and junior. As a senior, he transferred to [[Mira Mesa Senior High School]] in [[San Diego, California]], where he played [[running back]] and defense. He was named first-team all-state and league offensive MVP.

==College career==
Gordon played [[college football]] at [[Stanford University]], where he redshirted in his freshman season in 2000. As a redshirt freshman in 2001, Gordon played defensive end and inside [[linebacker]]. In 2002, as a starter, Gordon had four sacks and two fumble recoveries. Gordon moved to defensive tackle for his final season in 2003, and finished his college career with 35 games (18 starts), 71 tackles, and seven sacks.

==Professional career==

===Cleveland Browns===
Gordon was selected by the [[Cleveland Browns]] in the fourth round (161st overall) in the [[2004 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2004/draft.htm |title=2004 NFL Draft Listing |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en |access-date=2023-05-06}}</ref> In his rookie season, he played in six games and posted ten tackles. His second season with the Browns was ended by a knee injury that ruled him out for the entire year.

===Denver Broncos===
Gordon was signed by the [[Denver Broncos]] to their practice squad on March 22, 2006, after being waived by the Browns. He played in all four preseason games before being waived on September 2, 2006. He was re-signed to the team's [[practice squad]] the next day, where he spent the entire season. Gordon made the Broncos' 53-man roster in 2007, and played in four games, recording 13 tackles, before being waived on November 6, 2007.

===Baltimore Ravens===
Gordon was signed to the practice squad of the [[Baltimore Ravens]] on November 21, 2007. He was promoted to the Ravens' 53-man roster on December 9 and played in one of the Ravens' final four games, recording three tackles. He was not tendered as a [[restricted free agent]] following the season but was re-signed in March 2008 and released on August 29, 2008.

===Tennessee Titans (first stint)===
Gordon was signed to the Titans practice squad on November 5, 2008. He was activated from the [[practice squad]] on December 20, 2008. Gordon recorded six tackles in the final two games for the Titans. He was waived on January 6, 2009, during the [[2008–09 NFL playoffs|playoffs]].

===Philadelphia Eagles===
On January 21, 2009, Gordon was signed to a future deal by the [[Philadelphia Eagles]]. He was placed on [[injured reserve]] on June 11 with a torn [[Achilles tendon]] and was released with an injury settlement on August 11.

===New England Patriots===
Gordon signed with the [[New England Patriots]] on April 21, 2010. On June 10, 2010, the Patriots released Gordon.

===Seattle Seahawks (first stint)===
Gordan signed with the [[Seattle Seahawks]] on August 18, 2010. He was released on September 4, 2010.

===Tennessee Titans (second stint)===
The Titans re-signed Gordon on October 5, 2010. He was released again on November 9, 2010.

===Houston Texans===
Gordon was signed to the practice squad of the [[Houston Texans]] on November 17, 2010. He was released three days later.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://profootballarchives.com/transactions/g/gord00210.html | title=Amon Gordon NFL Transactions | publisher=profootballarchives.com | accessdate=May 14, 2024}}</ref>

===Seattle Seahawks (second stint)===
The Seahawks re-signed Gordon on November 23, 2010.

===Kansas City Chiefs===
After his contract with Seattle expired, Gordon signed with the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] on August 6, 2011. Gordon had his first sack as a Chief, during the Chiefs/Patriots game. The Chiefs would go on to lose that game 34–3. The next week, Gordon had his second sack against the Steelers. The Chiefs would lose the game 13–9. Gordon finished the season with two sacks and 23 tackles.
In 2012, Gordon was released in the last rounds of roster cuts with the Chiefs.

==Personal life==
He resides in Oakland, California.

He has dementia and is not able to work.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-10-20 |title=NFL agrees to end 'race-norming' in settlement |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/32439093/nfl-agrees-end-race-based-adjustments-dementia-testing-used-evaluate-concussion-claims |access-date=2023-12-20 |website=ESPN.com|agency=Associated Press |language=en}}</ref>

'''Amobi Okoye''' {{Pronunciation|Ig-Amobi Okoy.ogg|help=no}} (born June 10, 1987) is a Nigerian former professional player of [[American football]] who was a [[defensive tackle]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Louisville Cardinals football|Louisville Cardinals]] and was selected by the [[Houston Texans]] tenth overall in the [[2007 NFL draft]], the youngest player in NFL history to be drafted in the first round at 19. He was also a member of the [[Chicago Bears]], [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]], [[Dallas Cowboys]], and [[Saskatchewan Roughriders]].

==Early life==
Okoye was born in [[Anambra State]], Nigeria,<ref>{{Cite news |date=July 27, 2007 |title=Texans Sign Top Pick Okoye, Free Agent McCardell |work=Sports Network (via KFOXTV.com) |url=http://www.kfoxtv.com/nfl/13768163/detail.html |access-date=January 14, 2008}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Amobi Okoye |url=http://www.sportsline.com/nfl/players/draft/436548 |access-date=January 14, 2008 |website=NFLDraftScout.com (via Sportsline.com) |publisher=CBS}}</ref> a member of the [[Igbo people|Igbo ethnic group]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Jenkins |first=Lee |date=October 15, 2007 |title=No More Kid Stuff |url=https://vault.si.com/vault/2007/10/15/no-more-kid-stuff/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120719113712/http://vault.sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1108124/2/index.htm |archive-date=July 19, 2012 |access-date=January 26, 2009 |publisher=Time Inc}}</ref> He moved to [[Huntsville, Alabama]] in the United States when he was 12 years old.<ref name="espnthemag">{{Cite web |date=April 15, 2007 |title=Huge for His Size |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/draft07/news/story?id=2830642 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070919095115/http://sports.espn.go.com/nfl/draft07/news/story?id=2830642 |archive-date=September 19, 2007 |access-date=September 15, 2007 |publisher=ESPN The Magazine}}</ref> After only spending two weeks in middle school, he tested into the 9th grade.<ref name="espnthemag" /> He first started playing football as a sophomore at [[Lee High School (Huntsville, Alabama)|Lee High School]], knowing virtually nothing about the game before his high school coach suggested he go play ''[[Madden NFL]]'' football to learn.<ref name="espnthemag" /> By the time he was a senior, he won first-team All-State honors as both a defensive tackle and offensive tackle.  Because he shares the same surname as former [[Kansas City Chiefs]] fullback [[Christian Okoye]], some sources have claimed that the two are related.  Amobi says they are not related, but the two families live on adjoining land in Nigeria.<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 27, 2003 |title=Amobi Okoye may see action |url=http://louisville.scout.com/2/172370.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716021310/http://louisville.scout.com/2/172370.html |archive-date=July 16, 2011 |access-date=December 30, 2010 |publisher=Scout.com}}</ref>

==College career==
At age 15 Okoye chose the [[University of Louisville]] over [[Harvard University|Harvard]],<ref>{{Cite news |last=Manfull |first=Megan |date=April 28, 2007 |title=Texans select Louisville DT Amobi Okoye |work=[[Houston Chronicle]] |url=http://www.chron.com/disp/story.mpl/sports/4757683.html}}</ref> citing a desire to play for a strong football program.

At Louisville, Okoye majored in [[biology]]. He later switched his major to [[psychology]] and graduated a semester early, thereby completing his degree in three and a half years. At 16, he became the youngest player in the NCAA. Okoye played in all 13 games as a [[true freshman]] at defensive tackle and was credited with 17 tackles and a sack. He recorded then-career-best three tackles against [[Tulane Green Wave|Tulane]] and recorded his first career sack against [[University of Texas at El Paso|UTEP]].

As a sophomore, Okoye appeared in 11 of 12 games, recording 26 tackles and a sack. Okoye's only missed game was against [[East Carolina Pirates football|East Carolina]], because of a shoulder injury. Okoye also made his first collegiate start against [[Army Black Knights football|Army]], recording a career-high seven tackles.

In his junior season of 2005, he recorded 23 tackles and four tackles for a loss. In the biggest game of the year, against the [[2005 West Virginia Mountaineers football team|West Virginia Mountaineers]], Okoye recorded four tackles. He missed the [[Florida Atlantic Owls football|Florida Atlantic]] matchup due to a foot sprain. Against [[Kentucky Wildcats|Kentucky]], Okoye registered two tackles and a fumble recovery. Okoye also totaled three tackles against [[South Florida Bulls football|South Florida]].

As a senior in 2006, Okoye finally started all 13 games. In those 13 games, he registered 55 tackles, eight sacks, and recovered three fumbles. Okoye garnered [[Associated Press]] Second-team All-American honors and first-team All-[[Big East Conference (1979–2013)|Big East]] honors. As the [[NCAA|NCAA's]] youngest senior at 19 years old, Okoye garnered first-round draft status during the season. Okoye was invited to and performed in the [[Senior Bowl]].

===Houston Texans===
[[File:AmobiOkoye.jpg|thumb|250px|left|Okoye in 2007 while with the Texans]]
Okoye was selected by the [[Houston Texans]] in the first round of the [[2007 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2007 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2007/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-10 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He is still the youngest player to ever be drafted in the first round of the NFL Draft at only 19 years. [[Tremaine Edmunds]] became the second youngest at 19 years 11 months 26 days old, in 2018, making them the only two teenagers ever drafted in NFL history. He was the highest draft pick to come out of the University of Louisville since the [[AFL-NFL merger]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=NFL Draft History | website=[[NFL.com]] |url=http://www.nfl.com/draft/history/fulldraft?abbr=L&collegeName=Louisville&abbrFlag=0&type=school |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071022180431/http://www.nfl.com/draft/history/fulldraft?abbr=L&collegeName=Louisville&abbrFlag=0&type=school |archive-date=October 22, 2007 |access-date=October 1, 2007}}</ref>

Okoye signed a five-year deal with the Texans on July 26, which allowed him to begin training camp with his teammates the next day. With his first start, Okoye became the youngest player to appear in an NFL game since 1967.<ref name="espn">{{Cite news |date=September 9, 2007 |title=Williams recovers fumble for TD, has two sacks in win - Game Notes |work=ESPN.com |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/recap?gameId=270909034 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190113063124/http://www.espn.com/nfl/recap?gameId=270909034 |url-status=dead |archive-date=January 13, 2019 |access-date=September 9, 2007}}</ref>

Okoye was named Defensive Rookie of the Month for September 2007 after leading the AFC with four sacks.  He is the youngest player ever to receive the award.<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 30, 2012 |title=Okoye named NFL Defensive Rookie of the Month |url=http://www.houstontexans.com/news/Story.asp?story_id=3718 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071012112047/http://www.houstontexans.com/news/Story.asp?story_id=3718 |archive-date=October 12, 2007 |access-date=September 4, 2012 |publisher=HoustonTexans.com}}</ref>

On July 30, 2011, after four seasons in Houston, he was released.

===Chicago Bears (first stint)===
Okoye signed with the [[Chicago Bears]] on July 30, 2011.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Official Website of the Chicago Bearss |url=http://www.chicagobears.com/DailyBlogs.asp?DAILY_BLOG_DATE=07/30/11 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120722064415/http://www.chicagobears.com/DailyBlogs.asp?DAILY_BLOG_DATE=07/30/11 |archive-date=July 22, 2012 |access-date=September 4, 2012 |publisher=Chicagobears.com |df=mdy-all}}</ref> During the [[2011 Chicago Bears season]], Okoye played 16 games with one start, recording four sacks and 27 combined tackles.

===Tampa Bay Buccaneers===
Okoye signed with the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] on April 7, 2012.<ref>{{cite web | last=Dickerson | first=Jeff | title=Source: Bucs, Okoye agree to one-year deal | website=ESPN.com | date=2012-04-08 | url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/7787701/2012-nfl-free-agency-tampa-bay-buccaneers-agree-amobi-okoye-source-says | access-date=2025-08-05}}</ref> He was released by the team on August 31, before the start of the [[2012 NFL season]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Cummings |first=Roy |date=August 31, 2012 |title=Bucs release Okoye, others ahead of Friday roster deadline |work=[[The Tampa Tribune]] |url=http://www.tbo.com/sports/bucs/bucs-release-okoye-others-ahead-of-friday-roster-deadline-479754 |url-status=dead |access-date=November 27, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201044507/http://www.tbo.com/sports/bucs/bucs-release-okoye-others-ahead-of-friday-roster-deadline-479754 |archive-date=December 1, 2017}}</ref>

===Chicago Bears (second stint)===
Okoye returned to the Bears on August 31, 2012,<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 31, 2012 |title=Amobi Okoye to return to Bears - Chicago Sun-Times |url=http://www.suntimes.com/sports/14847776-419/amobi-okoye-to-return-to-bears.html |access-date=September 4, 2012 |publisher=Suntimes.com}}</ref> and signed a one-year contract on September 3.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mayer |first=Larry |title=Okoye thrilled to return to Bears |url=http://www.chicagobears.com/news/article-1/Okoye-thrilled-to-return-to-Bears/fbd972cc-b6fb-4bf6-b6a4-ee973845cfc2 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120906022134/http://www.chicagobears.com/news/article-1/Okoye-thrilled-to-return-to-Bears/fbd972cc-b6fb-4bf6-b6a4-ee973845cfc2 |archive-date=September 6, 2012 |access-date=September 4, 2012 |publisher=Chicagobears.com}}</ref> He was waived on November 27,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mayer |first=Larry |date=November 27, 2012 |title=Bears add veteran Gurode to offensive line |url=http://www.chicagobears.com/news/article-1/Bears-add-veteran-Gurode-to-offensive-line/d4f20455-135a-4dca-ad32-6ce38a682e5a |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121130090903/http://www.chicagobears.com/news/article-1/Bears-add-veteran-Gurode-to-offensive-line/d4f20455-135a-4dca-ad32-6ce38a682e5a |archive-date=November 30, 2012 |access-date=November 27, 2012 |publisher=[[Chicago Bears]]}}</ref> but was brought back on December 12.<ref>{{Cite web |date=December 12, 2012 |title=Report: Bears try out two quarterbacks |url=https://sports.yahoo.com/news/report-bears-try-two-quarterbacks-170013212--nfl.html |access-date=December 13, 2012 |publisher=[[Yahoo! Sports]]}}</ref> During the [[2012 Chicago Bears season]], Okoye played in nine games, recording one sack, one forced fumble, and 12 combined tackles.

===Dallas Cowboys===
After having missed the [[2013 NFL season]] due to what was referred to at the time as an "undisclosed medical issue", Okoye signed with the [[Dallas Cowboys]] on May 16, 2014.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Caplan |first=Adam |date=May 16, 2014 |title=Cowboys agree with Amobi Okoye |url=https://www.espn.com/dallas/nfl/story/_/id/10942222/dallas-cowboys-agree-2-year-deal-former-no-10-overall-pick-amobi-okoye |access-date=May 16, 2014 |website=[[ESPN]]}}</ref> On August 14, 2014, more details were revealed regarding his medical situation. Okoye had been diagnosed in March 2013 with [[anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis]] and had been placed in a [[medically induced coma]] to stabilize recurring [[seizures]]. He was cleared by doctors to play again, and is the first football player to attempt to come back from the disease.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Archer |first=Todd |title=Amobi Okoye of Dallas Cowboys intent on unprecedented return |url=https://www.espn.com/dallas/nfl/story/_/id/11355661/amobi-okoye-dallas-cowboys-intent-unprecedented-return |access-date=August 16, 2014 |website=ESPN.com |date=August 15, 2014 |publisher=ESPN Internet Ventures}}</ref>

On April 8, 2015, Okoye was released by the Cowboys.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hanzus |first=Dan |date=April 8, 2015 |title=Dallas Cowboys release Amobi Okoye |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/dallas-cowboys-release-amobi-okoye-0ap3000000484337 |access-date=April 8, 2015 |website=NFL.com}}</ref>

===Saskatchewan Roughriders===
In July 2016, Okoye signed a contract with the [[Saskatchewan Roughriders]] of the [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL), and was placed on the team's suspended (inactive) list.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dunk |first=Justin |date=July 7, 2016 |title=Former top-10 NFL draft pick signs with Riders |url=http://3downnation.com/2016/07/07/2007-nfl-top-10-pic-dl-amobi-okoye-signs-riders/ |access-date=November 27, 2016 |website=3 Down Nation}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=TRANSACTIONS – 2016 |url=https://www.cfl.ca/transactions-2016/ |access-date=November 27, 2017 |website=CFL.ca |archive-date=August 24, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170824185410/https://www.cfl.ca/transactions-2016/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> His contract with the team expired in February 2017.<ref>{{Cite web |title=CFL TRANSACTIONS |url=https://www.cfl.ca/transactions/ |access-date=November 27, 2017 |website=CFL.ca}}</ref>

'''Alvin D. Reed''' (born August 1, 1944) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[tight end]] in the [[American Football League]] (AFL) and [[National Football League]] (NFL).<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-houston-chronicle/176863285/ | title=Reed Speaks With Talent | work=[[The Houston Chronicle]] | date=October 31, 1969 | accessdate=17 July 2025 | author=Lundgren, Hal}}</ref> The 6 ft 5 in (1.96 m) 232 lb (105.2 kg) [[tight end]] from [[Prairie View A&M University]] was signed as a free agent by the AFL's [[Houston Oilers]] in 1967. Reed played nine seasons in professional football, from 1967 to 1975.

== Early life ==
Reed was born on August 1, 1944, in [[Kilgore, Texas]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Alvin Reed Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/R/ReedAl00.htm |access-date=2025-11-05 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He was one of Vesta Mae Loyd's eight children from two marriages. His maternal grandfather Virgil Lacy was the biggest influence in Reed's life, after his mother. The family was extremely poor, and his mother did maid work and took in washing and ironing to feed her family. He did not attend school one year for lack of adequate clothing. Reed attended C. B. Dansby High School in Kilgore, where he was a star lineman on offense and defense for the [[High school football|football]] team.<ref name=":8">{{Cite news |last=Franks |first=Zarko |date=July 18, 1971 |title=Kilgore's Reed Really Gentle Soul |work=Kilgore News Herald (Kilgore, Texas) |pages=7 |agency=The Houston Chronicle}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite news |last=Inman |first=John |date=June 4, 1974 |title=Reed Performs without Fanfare |work=The Kilgore News Herald |pages=2}}</ref> Dansby was a [[Racial segregation|segregated school]], and was originally called Kilgore Colored High School until 1956, ceasing operations after the local high schools integrated in 1970.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Katz |first=Chelsea |date=November 16, 2016 |title=Dansby marker submitted for state approval |work=Kilgore News Herald |pages=1, 3}}</ref> 

Reed also was a leading scorer on the school's [[High school basketball|basketball]] team, and a champion member of its [[Track and field|track]] team. In the 1962-63 season, he led Dansby and the district in scoring (18.8 [[points per game]] on the season and 18 points per game in district games), and was named to the District 3-AAA All-Star basketball team. In 1961, he was first in the district and the state in the [[shot put]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=December 21, 1960 |title=Scott Nets 50–30 Win |work=Tyler Morning Telegraph (Tyler, Texas) |pages=1, Sec. 2}}</ref><ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite news |date=February 14, 1963 |title=Two Dansby Players In All-Star Tilt; Dansby Girls Meet All-Star Squad |work=The Kilgore News Herald (Kilgore, Texas) |pages=4}}</ref> He also received a science fair award in biology during high school, as well as an award for singing in the high school octet.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last=Williams |first=Dorothy L. |date=June 2, 1961 |title=Longview, Texas |work=The Call (Kansas City, Missouri) |pages=14}}</ref>

== College career ==
Reed attended [[Prairie View A&M University]] on a football scholarship, and was able to make it through college with those funds and financial help from his grandfather. He studied industrial education, with a major in drafting.<ref name=":4" /> As a freshman in 1963, he started on the defensive line at [[Defensive end|left end]] for Prairie View.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news |date=December 13, 1963 |title=Johnnies vs. Panthers |work=The Sacramento Bee |pages=D1}}</ref> His teammates included future [[American Football League]] (AFL) and [[National Football League]] (NFL) [[All-Pro]] receiver [[Otis Taylor (American football)|Otis Taylor]] and future Hall of Fame defensive back [[Ken Houston]].<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Otis Taylor Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/T/TaylOt00.htm |access-date=2025-11-05 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Ken Houston {{!}} Pro Football Hall of Fame |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/players/ken-houston |access-date=2025-11-05 |website=pfhof |language=en}}</ref> Their [[1963 Prairie View A&M Panthers football team|1963 team]] reached the [[NAIA football national championship|NAIA (National Association of Intercollegiate Athletics) championship game]], losing to [[College of Saint Benedict and Saint John's University|St. John's of Minnesota]] in the [[Camellia Bowl (1961–1980)|Camelia Bowl]], 33–27.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-11-05 |title=Take Me Back Tuesday: The 1963 National Championship |url=https://gojohnnies.com/news/2020/5/26/football-take-me-back-tuesday-the-1963-national-championship.aspx |access-date=2025-11-05 |website=Saint John's University Athletics |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=December 15, 1963 |title=Prairie View Beaten, 33–27 |work=The Houston Chronicle |pages=2, Sec. 7 |agency=United Press International}}</ref>

In 1964, Reed played end, and also served as the team's [[placekicker]]. He was used as an offensive end during that season.<ref>{{Cite news |last=McElroy |first=George |date=October 4, 1964 |title=Prairie View Rambles Past Grambling, 22–14 |work=The Houston Post |pages=10, Sec. 4}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=McElroy |first=George |date=October 10, 1964 |title=Prairie View 2 TD Favorite Over TSU |work=The Houston Post |pages=2, Sec. 4}}</ref> Reed became a full time [[tight end]] during his junior and senior years, but was seldom a pass receiving target; Otis Taylor being the principal pass receiver.<ref name=":4" /><ref>{{Cite news |date=October 3, 1965 |title=Grambling Bombs Prairie View, 44–7 |work=Monroe Morning World (Monroe, Louisiana) |pages=8-B}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite news |last=Hollis |first=John |date=July 23, 1970 |title=Reed model for all free agents |work=The Houston Post |pages=6, Sec. 4}}</ref> As a senior in 1966, Reed, now a 6 ft 4 in (1.93 m) 230 lb (104.3 kg) receiver, was named one of Prairie View's three captains.<ref>{{Cite news |date=October 1, 1966 |title=Prairie View Builds Under New Direction |work=The Pittsburgh Courier |pages=13}}</ref>   

== Professional career ==

=== Houston Oilers ===
Reed was not drafted in 1967, and signed as a free agent with the [[Houston Oilers]] in March 1967.<ref>{{Cite news |date=March 30, 1967 |title=Oilers Sign 4 More Players |work=The Houston Post |pages=6, Sec. 5}}</ref><ref name=":3" /> The Oilers' Tom Williams had convinced Reed to try out for the team.<ref name=":4" /> Houston's director of player personnel, Charley Hall, stated that Reed went undrafted because few passes were thrown to him in college and Reed did not demonstrate a facility for catching passes or running with a smooth gait as a receiver. However, Reed was a determined and hard worker, with a great desire to improve; and Oilers' receiver coach [[Hugh Devore]] and veteran receiver [[Lionel Taylor]] put in extra time with Reed to improve his skills.<ref name=":3" /> Later in his career, after being traded from the Oilers, Reed expressed his gratitude to Oilers' coach [[Wally Lemm]] for giving Reed the opportunity to play in his first season.<ref name=":4" />

Reed made the team as a [[tight end]], and started eight games in 1967, with 11 receptions for 144 yards.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Twombly |first=Wells |date=September 17, 1967 |title=Oiler Ground Game Feared |work=The Houston Chronicle |pages=6, Sec. 6}}</ref> The Oilers lost the [[1967 American Football League Championship Game|1967 AFL Championship Game]] to the [[1967 Oakland Raiders season|Oakland Raiders]], 40–7; with Reed catching four passes for 60 yards.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Championship - Houston Oilers at Oakland Raiders - December 31st, 1967 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/196712310rai.htm |access-date=2025-11-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>  

In 1968, Reed started 13 games at tight end, with 46 receptions for 747 yards and five touchdowns.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1968 Houston Oilers Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/oti/1968.htm |access-date=2025-11-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He was eighth in the AFL in receiving yards and ninth in receptions.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1968 AFL Leaders and Leaderboards |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1968_AFL/leaders.htm |access-date=2025-11-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He was second to [[Jim Whalen]] of the [[New England Patriots|Boston Patriots]] for most receptions by a tight end.<ref name=":3" /> Reed was selected to play in the 1968 [[American Football League All-Star game|All-Star game]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1968 AFL Pro Bowlers |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1968_AFL/probowl.htm |access-date=2025-11-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He was named first-team [[American Football League All-League Team|All-AFL]] by [[The Sporting News|''The Sporting News'']] and second-team All-AFL by the [[Associated Press]] (AP) and [[United Press International]] (UPI).<ref>{{Cite web |title=1968 AFL Pro Bowlers |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1968_AFL/probowl.htm |access-date=2025-11-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

Reed was an All-Star again in 1969, the last season before the [[AFL–NFL merger|AFL-NFL merger]]. ''The Sporting News'' again named him first-team All-AFL at tight end, and the AP, UPI and [[Newspaper Enterprise Association]] (NEA), among other entities, named him second-team All-AFL.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1969 AFL Pro Bowlers |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1969_AFL/probowl.htm |access-date=2025-11-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=General History - Chronology (1960 to 1979) {{!}} Pro Football Hall of Fame |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/football-history/general-history-chronology-1960-to-1979 |access-date=2025-10-30 |website=pfhof |language=en}}</ref> He started all 14 games, with a career-high 51 receptions for 664 yards and two touchdowns.<ref name=":2" /> He was fourth in the AFL in receptions that season,<ref>{{Cite web |title=1969 AFL Leaders and Leaderboards |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1969_AFL/leaders.htm |access-date=2025-11-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> and led all AFL tight ends in receptions.<ref name=":3" /> The Oilers lost in the [[1969 American Football League playoffs|divisional round of the playoffs]] to the [[1969 Oakland Raiders season|Oakland Raiders]], 56–7, with Reed scoring the only Oilers' touchdown, and catching a team-leading seven passes for 81 yards.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Divisional Round - Houston Oilers at Oakland Raiders - December 21st, 1969 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/196912210rai.htm |access-date=2025-11-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

In 1970, Reed started 13 games for the Oilers, with 47 receptions for 604 yards and two touchdowns.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |title=1970 Houston Oilers Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/oti/1970.htm |access-date=2025-11-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> His 47 receptions were tied for 10th best in the NFL.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1970 NFL Receiving |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1970/receiving.htm |access-date=2025-11-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> In 1971, he started 10 games and had 25 receptions; and in 1972, Reed started all 14 Oilers' games, with 19 receptions.<ref name=":2" /> The Oilers were, 3–10–1 in 1970, 4–9–1 in 1971 and 1–13 in 1972.<ref name=":7" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=1971 Houston Oilers Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/oti/1971.htm |access-date=2025-11-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=1972 Houston Oilers Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/oti/1972.htm |access-date=2025-11-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

As an Oiler (1967–72), Reed had 199 receptions for 2,818 (14.2 yards per reception), and 11 receiving touchdowns.<ref name=":2" />

=== Washington Redskins ===
The Oilers had selected Reed's Prairie View teammate [[Ken Houston]] with the ninth pick in the 1967 NFL draft, and Reed and Houston were teammates on the Oilers from 1967 to 1972.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1967 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1967/draft.htm |access-date=2025-11-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=Ken Houston Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/H/HousKe02.htm |access-date=2025-11-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> On May 15, 1972, Oilers general manager [[Sid Gillman]] traded Houston to the [[Washington Commanders|Washington Redskins]] and coach [[George Allen (American football coach)|George Allen]] for five players and a draft choice. Two weeks later Gillman and Allen engineered a trade sending Reed to Washington for a draft pick.<ref>{{Cite news |date=May 29, 1973 |title=Oilers Deal Reed To Washington |work=The Blade (Toledo, Ohio) |pages=33 |agency=Associated Press}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite news |last=Snyder |first=Jimmy |date=September 11, 1973 |title=Jimmy The Greek's Preseason Pro Football Special, Allen's trades making Redskins sound team |work=Birmingham Post-Herald (Birmingham, Alabama) |pages=9}}</ref> Reed and Houston would play three more years together in Washington (1973 to 1975).<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":5" />

In 1973, Reed was intended to serve as a backup to All Pro tight end [[Jerry Smith (tight end)|Jerry Smith]]. However, when Smith suffered a preseason injury, Reed stepped in to start five games, and had nine receptions for 124 yards in those games. However, he suffered a knee injury that caused him to miss the season's final nine games.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jerry Smith Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/S/SmitJe01.htm |access-date=2025-11-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":4" /><ref name=":6" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=1973 Washington Redskins Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/was/1973.htm |access-date=2025-11-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He played two more seasons for Washington (1974-75), but did not start any games. Reed had four receptions and one touchdown catch in 1974,<ref>{{Cite web |title=1974 Washington Redskins Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/was/1974.htm |access-date=2025-11-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> and two receptions in 1975, both for touchdowns.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1975 Washington Redskins Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/was/1975.htm |access-date=2025-11-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Washington released him in late August 1976.<ref>{{Cite news |date=August 27, 1976 |title=Redskins release Biggs, Reed |work=The Free Lance-Star (Fredericksburg, Virginia) |pages=10}}</ref>

== Honors ==
In 1992, Reed was inducted into the Prairie View A&M University Sports Hall of Fame.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Alvin Reed (1992) - Prairie View A&M University Sports Hall Of Fame |url=https://pvpanthers.com/honors/prairie-view-am-university-sports-hall-of-fame/alvin-reed/66 |access-date=2025-11-05 |website=Prairie View A&M University Athletics |language=en}}</ref> In 1999, he was inducted into the Southwest Athletic Conference Hall of Fame.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Alvin Reed (1999) - Hall of Fame |url=https://swac.org/hof.aspx?hof=229 |access-date=2025-11-06 |website=swac.org |language=en}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
During his time in Houston, Reed worked in the offseason for the Houston Skill Center, as a job training evaluator for those being trained in job skills. This included performing work for [[NASA]].<ref name=":8" />

'''Amos Lawrence Jr.''' (born January 9, 1958) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] for the [[San Francisco 49ers]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[North Carolina Tar Heels football|North Carolina Tar Heels]] and was selected in the fourth round of the [[1981 NFL draft]].

== Early life ==
Lawrence was raised in the Diggs Park housing project in [[Norfolk, Virginia]].<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Ch |first1=Charles |last2=ler |date=1988-10-31 |title=NO LONGER 'FAMOUS AMOS,' LAWRENCE BACK IN GHETTO |language=en-US |newspaper=Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1988/10/31/no-longer-famous-amos-lawrence-back-in-ghetto/8790b037-4554-4e6f-b5a1-0c0a5b797ef3/ |access-date=2022-07-24 |issn=0190-8286}}</ref>

== Career ==
Lawrence was selected by the [[San Diego Chargers]] out of the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]] in the fourth round of the [[1981 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=TarHeelIllustrated - No. 2: Amos Lawrence |url=https://northcarolina.rivals.com/news/no-2-amos-lawrence-1 |access-date=2022-07-24 |website=northcarolina.rivals.com|date=29 May 2021 }}</ref> On September 10, 1981, Lawrence was traded to the [[San Francisco 49ers]] for a fourth round pick in the [[1984 NFL draft]]. He was later cut during training camp. Lawrence joined the [[Pittsburgh Maulers (1984)|Pittsburgh Maulers]] in 1984 but was cut from the team after [[Mike Rozier]] was signed. He later briefly played for the [[Jacksonville Bulls]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=FAMOUS AMOS: A RICHES-TO-RAGS TALE |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/ct-xpm-1988-12-04-8802220782-story.html |access-date=2022-07-24 |website=Chicago Tribune}}</ref>

After his professional career ended, Lawrence returned to Norfolk, where he worked busing tables and sorting newspapers, among other odd jobs. His high school football coach, Bert Harrell, got him a job as an attendance officer and junior varsity assistant coach at [[Lake Taylor High School]].

'''Alvoid Wilson Mays''' (born July 10, 1966) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[cornerback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). ==Professional career==
Mays was selected in the eighth round of the [[1989 NFL draft]] by the Houston Oilers. He was cut during [[Training camp (National Football League)|training camp]].

Mays scored his only touchdown on October 1, 1995, when he was with the Pittsburgh Steelers. In a game against the San Diego Chargers at Three Rivers Stadium, he intercepted a pass from Chargers Quarterback Stan Humphries & returned it for a touchdown.
